metadata.title: Whole Brain Susceptibility Mapping Using Harmonic Incompatibility Removal

TheTitle.expansion: Whole Brain Susceptibility Mapping Using Harmonic Incompatibility Removal

TheAuthors.expansion: Chenglong Bao, Jae Kyu Choi, and Bin Dong

nodes.name: Field-to-source inverse problem of QSM
nodes.statement: Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) aims to visualize the three dimensional susceptibility distribution by solving the field-to-source inverse problem using the phase data in magnetic resonance signal. However, the inverse problem is ill-posed since the Fourier transform of integral kernel has zeroes in the frequency domain.
nodes.statement_short: Recover the 3D magnetic susceptibility distribution from MR phase data, an ill-posed field-to-source deconvolution.

nodes.name: Complex GRE signal model
nodes.statement: \begin{align} I(\x,TE)=m(\x)\exp\left\{-i\left(b(\x)\omega_0B_0TE+\theta_0(\x)\right)\right\}, \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The observed gradient-echo signal is the magnitude image modulated by a phase linear in the total field.

nodes.name: Phase model of the GRE signal
nodes.statement: \begin{align} \theta(\x)=b(\x)\omega_0B_0TE+\theta_0(\x). \end{align}

nodes.name: Dipole convolution relation for dipole inversion
nodes.statement: Given the local field $b_l$, the dipole inversion recovers the susceptibility distribution $\chi$ in $\Om$ by solving the following convolution relation \cite{T.Liu2011,T.Liu2011a,T.Liu2009}: \begin{align} b_l(\x)=\pv\int_{\Om}d(\x-\y)\chi(\y)\rd\y, \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The local field is the principal-value convolution of the susceptibility with the dipole kernel over the ROI.

nodes.name: Dipole kernel $d$
nodes.statement: where $\pv$ denotes the principal value \cite{E.M.Stein2011} of the singular integral with the kernel $d$: \begin{align*} d(\x)=\f{2x_3^2-x_1^2-x_2^2}{4\pi|\x|^5}. \end{align*}
nodes.origin_citation: E. M. Stein 2011; de Rochefort et al. 2010

nodes.name: Dipole inversion in the frequency domain
nodes.statement: \begin{align} \msF(b_l)(\xxi)=\mD(\xxi)\msF(\chi)(\xxi)=\left(\f{1}{3}-\f{\xi_3^2}{|\xxi|^2}\right)\msF(\chi)(\xxi) \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: In Fourier space the field is the susceptibility multiplied by $\mD(\xxi)=1/3-\xi_3^2/|\xxi|^2$.
nodes.origin_citation: de Rochefort et al. 2010; Haacke et al. 2015

nodes.name: Critical manifold $\Gamma_0$
nodes.statement: From \eqref{QSM_Fou}, it is easy to see that recovering the susceptibility distribution $\chi$ is ill-posed as $\mD=0$ on the critical manifold $\Gamma_0=\left\{\xxi\in\R^3:\xi_1^2+\xi_2^2-2\xi_3^2=0\right\}$.
nodes.statement_short: The cone in frequency space where the dipole kernel vanishes, the source of ill-posedness.

nodes.name: Truncated K-space division (TKD)
nodes.statement: One benchmark method, called the truncated K-space division (TKD) \cite{K.Shmueli2009}, finds the approximate solution to \cref{QSM_Fou} via: \begin{align} \chi_{\hbar}=\msF^{-1}(\mX_{\hbar}),~~~\text{where}~~\mX_{\hbar}(\xxi)=\f{\mathrm{sign}(\mD(\xxi))}{\max\left\{|\mD(\xxi)|,\hbar\right\}}\msF(b_l)(\xxi) \end{align} with a threshold level $\hbar>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct inversion that clips the dipole kernel away from zero before dividing in k-space.

nodes.name: Tikhonov regularization for QSM
nodes.statement: Another method recovers $\chi$ via solving the following Tikhonov regularization \cite{B.Kressler2010}: \begin{align} \min_{\chi}~\f{1}{2}\left\|A\chi-b_l\right\|_2^2+\eps\left\|\chi\right\|_2^2 \end{align} where $\eps>0$ and $A$ denotes the forward operator that is obtained by discretizing the kernel $\mD$.
nodes.statement_short: Least-squares dipole inversion with an $\ell_2$ penalty on the susceptibility.

nodes.name: Regularization based QSM reconstruction model
nodes.statement: Mathematically, it is formulated as solving the minimization problem: \begin{align} \min_{\chi}~F(b_l|\chi)+R(\chi), \end{align} where $F(b_l|\chi)$ denotes the data fidelity term and $R(\chi)$ is the regularization term which mostly promotes the sparse approximation of $\chi$ under some linear transformation such as total variation and wavelet frames.
nodes.statement_short: Generic QSM reconstruction as data fidelity plus a sparsity-promoting regularizer.
nodes.origin_citation: Y. Kee et al. 2017; S. Wang & Liu 2013

nodes.name: QSM partial differential equation
nodes.statement: The differential approaches are based on the following partial differential equation (PDE) \begin{align} -\Delta b_l(\x)=P(D)\chi(\x)=\left(-\f{1}{3}\Delta+\f{\p^2}{\p x_3^2}\right)\chi(\x)~~~~~~~\x\in\Om \end{align} which is derived from the Maxwell's equation \cite{E.M.Haacke1999,J.K.Seo2014}.
nodes.statement_short: The local field and susceptibility satisfy $-\Delta b_l=P(D)\chi$ inside the ROI.

nodes.name: Integral approach with spherical mean value (SMV) filter
nodes.statement: In \cite{Y.Kee2017}, the differential approach is implemented by incorporating the spherical mean value (SMV) filter $S_r$ with a radius $r>0$ \cite{W.Li2014} into the integral approach: \begin{align} \min_{\chi}~\f{1}{2}\left\|S_r\left(A\chi-b_l\right)\right\|_2^2+R(\chi). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Integral-approach reconstruction whose fidelity term is filtered by an SMV kernel of radius $r$.
nodes.origin_citation: Y. Kee et al. 2017; W. Li et al. 2014

nodes.name: Harmonic incompatibility
nodes.statement: Whenever the data acquisition is based on the PDE \cref{QSM_PDE}, the measured local field data will be written as the superposition of $b_l$ in \cref{QSM_Deconv} and the ambiguity of $-\Delta$, which will be referred as the \emph{harmonic incompatibility}.
nodes.statement_short: The $-\Delta$-ambiguity superposed on the measured local field, on top of the true dipole-inversion field.

nodes.name: Magnetostatic Maxwell's equation
nodes.statement:
This magnetization generates a macroscopic field $\B(\x)$ satisfying the following magnetostatic Maxwell's equation \cite{E.M.Haacke1999,J.K.Seo2014}  egin{align}  egin{split} 
a\cdot\B&=0\ 
a	imes\B&=\mu_0
a	imes\M, \end{split} \end{align} where $\mu_0=8.854	imes 10^{-12} \mathrm{F/m}$ is the vacuum permittivity.

nodes.name: Lorenz sphere correction model
nodes.statement: we use the following Lorenz sphere correction model \cite{E.M.Haacke1999}: \begin{align} \B_{\ell}(\x)=\B(\x)-\f{2}{3}\mu_0\M(\x) \end{align} to relate $\B(\x)$ and $\B_{\ell}(\x)$.

nodes.name: Linear-material approximation of the susceptibility
nodes.statement: Moreover, since we consider the linear magnetic materials with $|\chi|\ll1$, $\chi$ can be approximated as \begin{align} \chi(\x)\approx\f{\mu_0}{B_0}\M(\x). \end{align}

nodes.name: Total field $b$
nodes.statement: Finally, we introduce the total field $b(\x)$ as \begin{align} b(\x)=\f{B_{\ell3}(\x)-B_0}{B_0} \end{align} where $B_{\ell3}(\x)$ denotes the third component of $\B_{\ell}(\x)$.

nodes.name: Frequency-domain relation between $\chi$ and $b$
nodes.statement: we obtain the following relation between $\chi$ and $b$ in the frequency domain: \begin{align} |\xxi|^2\msF(b)(\xxi)=\left(\f{1}{3}|\xxi|^2-\xi_3^2\right)\msF(\chi)(\xxi), \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Combining Maxwell, Lorenz correction and the linear approximation gives the k-space field-source relation.

nodes.name: QSM PDE $-\Delta b=P(D)\chi$
nodes.statement: \begin{align} -\Delta b=P(D)\chi:=\left(-\f{1}{3}\Delta+\f{\p^2}{\p x_3^2}\right)\chi. \end{align}

nodes.name: General bounded solution of the QSM PDE
nodes.statement: Then for a given susceptibility distribution $\chi$ (in $\R^3$), the general solution $b$ which is bounded everywhere in $\R^3$ is expressed as \begin{align} b(\x)=\int_{\R^3}\Phi(\x-\y)\left(-\f{1}{3}\Delta_{\y}+\f{\p^2}{\p y_3^2}\right)\chi(\y)\rd\y+b_0 \end{align} where $b_0$ is some constant, and $\Phi(\x)=1/\left(4\pi|\x|\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Every bounded solution is the Newtonian potential of $P(D)\chi$ plus a constant $b_0$.

nodes.name: Forward model for the total field ($b_0=0$)
nodes.statement: we assume that $b_0=0$ and \begin{align} b(\x)=\int_{\R^3}\Phi(\x-\y)\left(-\f{1}{3}\Delta_{\y}+\f{\p^2}{\p y_3^2}\right)\chi(\y)\rd\y \end{align} in the rest of this paper.
nodes.statement_short: The forward model used throughout: the total field is the Newtonian potential of $P(D)\chi$ over all of $\R^3$.

nodes.name: Equivalence of the potential and principal-value forward models
nodes.statement: Since \cite[Proposition A.1.]{J.K.Choi2014} has discussed the equivalence between \cref{Forward1} and the following representation in the literature \begin{align} b(\x)=\pv\int_{\R^3}d(\x-\y)\chi(\y)\rd\y, \end{align} we shall use \cref{Forward1} in the rest of this paper. Note that \cref{Forward1} avoids the singularity of the kernel $d(\x-\y)$ in \cref{Forward_Convention} as $\Phi(\x-\y)$ is locally integrable near $\x=\y$.
nodes.statement_short: The potential form is used because it avoids the singular dipole kernel of the principal-value form.

nodes.name: Poisson's equation for background field removal
nodes.statement: the background field removal methods take the form of the following Poisson's equation in \cite{D.Zhou2014}: \begin{align} \left\{\begin{array}{rcll} -\Delta b_l\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&-\Delta b&\text{in}~\Om \vspace{0.125em}\\ b_l\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&0&\text{on}~\p\Om. \end{array}\right. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Background field removal solves $-\Delta b_l=-\Delta b$ in $\Om$ with zero Dirichlet data on $\p\Om$.

nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data

Let $b$ satisfy \cref{Forward1} for a given $\chi$ compactly supported in $\R^3$
If we extend $b_l$ into $\R^3$ by assigning $b_l(\x)=0$ for $\x\notin\Om$
conclusions: There exists $v(x)$ such that \begin{align} b_l(\x)=\int_{\Om}\Phi(\x-\y)\left(-\f{1}{3}\Delta_{\y}+\f{\p^2}{\p y_3^2}\right)\chi(\y)\rd\y+v(\x) \end{align} for $\x\in\R^3$, and $v(\x)$ satisfies \begin{align} \int_{\R^3}v(\x)\left(-\Delta\varphi\right)(\x)\rd\x=\int_{\p\Om}\left[\f{\p v_{\mathrm i}}{\p\bn}(\x)-\f{\p v_{\mathrm e}}{\p\bn}(\x)\right]\varphi(\x)\rd\ssi(\x) \end{align} for $\varphi\in C_0^{\infty}(\R^3)$, where $v_{\mathrm i}$ and $v_{\mathrm e}$ denote the restriction of $v$ in $\overline{\Om}$ and $\R^3\setminus\Om$ respectively, and $\bn$ denotes the outward unit normal vector of $\p\Om$.
\f{\p v_{\mathrm i}}{\p\bn}-\f{\p v_{\mathrm e}}{\p\bn}\neq0~~~~\text{almost everywhere on}~\p\Om
Hence, $-\Delta v=0$ in $\R^3\setminus\p\Om$, and $-\Delta v\neq0$ on $\p\Om$ in this case.

nodes.name: Proof of the harmonic incompatibility characterization
nodes.statement: Since $-\Delta b=P(D)\chi$, the governing equation in \cref{LBV} becomes \begin{align*} \left\{\begin{array}{rcll} -\Delta b_l\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&P(D)\chi&\text{in}~\Om \vspace{0.125em}\\ b_l\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&0&\text{on}~\p\Om. \end{array}\right. \end{align*} Let $G(\x,\y)$ denote the Green's function in $\Om$: \begin{align*} G(\x,\y)=\Phi(\y-\x)-H(\x,\y) \end{align*} where for each $\x\in\Om$, the corrector function $H(\x,\y)$ satisfies \begin{align*} \left\{\begin{array}{rclll} -\Delta_{\y} H(\x,\y)\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&0&\text{if}&\y\in\Om \vspace{0.125em}\\ H(\x,\y)\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&\Phi(\y-\x)&\text{if}&\y\in\p\Om. \end{array}\right. \end{align*} Note that since $G(\x,\y)=G(\y,\x)$ for $\x,\y\in\Om$ and $\Phi(\y-\x)=\Phi(\x-\y)$, we have $H(\x,\y)=H(\y,\x)$ for $\x,\y\in\Om$. Consequently, we have \begin{align} -\Delta_{\x}H(\x,\y)=-\Delta_{\x}H(\y,\x)=0~~~~~\x\in\Om. \end{align} Then the solution to \cref{LBV} is represented as \begin{align*} b_l(\x)=\int_{\Om}G(\x,\y)P(D_{\y})\chi(\y)\rd\y=\int_{\Om}\Phi(\x-\y)P(D_{\y})\chi(\y)\rd\y+\mH(\x) \end{align*} where we used the fact that $\Phi(\y-\x)=\Phi(\x-\y)$, and $\mH(\x)$ is defined as \begin{align*} \mH(\x)=-\int_{\Om}H(\x,\y)P(D_{\y})\chi(\y)\rd\y \end{align*} for $\x\in\Om$. Then we can see that $\mH(\x)$ satisfies \begin{align} \left\{\begin{array}{rcll} -\Delta\mH\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&0&\text{in}~\Om \vspace{0.125em}\\ \mH\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&-\wt{b}_l&\text{on}~\p\Om \end{array}\right. \end{align} where the first equation of \cref{H_HarmonicEq} comes from \cref{CorrectorHarmonicSym}. Here, $\wt{b}_l$ is induced by the information of $\chi$ only in $\Om$: \begin{align} \wt{b}_l(\x)=\int_{\Om}\Phi(\x-\y)P(D_{\y})\chi(\y)\rd\y=\int_{\R^3}\Phi(\x-\y)1_{\Om}(\y)P(D_{\y})\chi(\y)\rd\y \end{align} with $1_{\Om}$ being the characteristic function of $\Om$. Based on the fact that $b_l(\x)=0$ for $\x\in\R^3\setminus\overline{\Om}$, we define \begin{align*} v(\x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cccll} v_{\mathrm i}(\x)\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&\mH(\x)&\text{if}&\x\in\Om \vspace{0.125em}\\ v_{\mathrm e}(\x)\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&-\wt{b}_l(\x)&\text{if}&\x\notin\Om. \end{array}\right. \end{align*} Hence, we obtain \cref{NewModeling}, and we can further see that $v_{\mathrm i}$ and $v_{\mathrm e}$ satisfy \begin{align} -\Delta v_{\mathrm i}&=0~~~~~~\text{in } \Om \\ -\Delta v_{\mathrm e}&=0~~~~~~\text{in } \R^3\setminus\overline{\Om} \\ v_{\mathrm i}=v_{\mathrm e}&=-\wt{b}_l~~~\text{on } \p\Om, \end{align} respectively, where \cref{v_eharmonic} comes from \cref{TrueLocalField}; $-\Delta\wt{b}_l=1_{\Om}P(D)\chi$, i.e. $-\Delta\wt{b}_l=P(D)\chi$ in $\Om$, and $-\Delta\wt{b}_l=0$ in $\R^3\setminus\overline{\Om}$. To prove \cref{DistLapIncompatibility}, let $\varphi\in C_0^{\infty}(\R^3)$, and we consider \begin{align*} \int_{\R^3}v(\x)\left(-\Delta\varphi\right)(\x)\rd\x&=\int_{\Om}v_{\mathrm i}(\x)\left(-\Delta\varphi\right)(\x)\rd\x+\int_{\R^3\setminus\overline{\Om}}v_{\mathrm e}(\x)\left(-\Delta\varphi\right)(\x)\rd\x\\ &=I_1+I_2 \end{align*} Using \cref{v_iharmonic,vboundaryconti} and the Green's identity (e.g. \cite{Evans2010}), we have \begin{align*} I_1&=\int_{\Om}\left[\varphi(\x)\left(\Delta v_{\mathrm i}\right)(\x)-v_{\mathrm i}(\x)\left(\Delta\varphi\right)(\x)\right]\rd\x\\ &=\int_{\p\Om}\left[\varphi(\x)\f{\p v_{\mathrm i}}{\p\bn}(\x)-v_{\mathrm i}(\x)\f{\p\varphi}{\p\bn}(\x)\right]\rd\ssi(\x)=\int_{\p\Om}\left[\varphi(\x)\f{\p v_{\mathrm i}}{\p\bn}(\x)+\wt{b}_l(\x)\f{\p\varphi}{\p\bn}(\x)\right]\rd\ssi(\x). \end{align*} Similarly using \cref{v_eharmonic,vboundaryconti}, we also have \begin{align*} I_2&=\int_{\R^3\setminus\overline{\Om}}\left[\varphi(\x)\left(\Delta v_{\mathrm e}\right)(\x)-v_{\mathrm e}(\x)\left(\Delta\varphi\right)(\x)\right]\rd\x\\ &=\int_{\p\Om}\left[-\varphi(\x)\f{\p v_{\mathrm e}}{\p\bn}(\x)+v_{\mathrm e}(\x)\f{\p\varphi}{\p\bn}(\x)\right]\rd\ssi(\x)=-\int_{\p\Om}\left[\varphi(\x)\f{\p v_{\mathrm e}}{\p\bn}(\x)+\wt{b}_l(\x)\f{\p\varphi}{\p\bn}(\x)\right]\rd\ssi(\x) \end{align*} where the second equality comes from the fact that we need to compute the inward normal derivatives on $\p\Om$. Hence, combining these two equalities, we obtain \cref{DistLapIncompatibility}. To prove 2, we assume on the contrary that there exists $\x\in\p\Om$ such that \begin{align*} \f{\p v_{\mathrm i}}{\p\bn}=\f{\p v_{\mathrm e}}{\p\bn} \end{align*} for some open and connected set $U\subseteq\p\Om$ such that $\x\in U$ and $\ssi(U)>0$. Choose $r>0$ such that $B(\x,r)\cap\p\Om$ is contained in $U$, where $B(\x,r)$ denotes an open ball centered at $\x$ with radius $r$. Then since $-\Delta v=0$ in $B(\x,r)$ and $v=v_{\mathrm e}=-\wt{b}_l$ in $B(\x,r)\cap\left(\R^3\setminus\overline{\Om}\right)$, it follows that $v=-\wt{b}_l$ in $B(\x,r)$ by the analyticity of $v$ in $B(\x,r)$. Since this means that $v=v_{\mathrm i}=-\wt{b}_l$ in $B(\x,r)\cap\Om$, together with the fact that $v_{\mathrm i}$ is harmonic in $\Om$, we have $v_{\mathrm i}=-\wt{b}_l$ in $\Om$ by the analyticity of $v_{\mathrm i}$ in $\Om$. Since $v=-\wt{b}_l$ on $\p\Om$, we have $v=-\wt{b}_l$ in $\R^3$. Hence, $-\Delta\wt{b}_l=0$ in $\R^3$, and thus, $P(D)\chi=0$ in $\Om$, which is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Green's-function representation splits $b_l$ into the true dipole field plus $v$; Green's identity gives the surface measure, and analytic continuation gives nonvanishing by contradiction.

nodes.name: Rewrite the boundary value problem with the source $P(D)\chi$
nodes.statement: Since $-\Delta b=P(D)\chi$, the governing equation in \cref{LBV} becomes \begin{align*} \left\{\begin{array}{rcll} -\Delta b_l\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&P(D)\chi&\text{in}~\Om \vspace{0.125em}\\ b_l\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&0&\text{on}~\p\Om. \end{array}\right. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the QSM PDE into the background-removal BVP.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data

nodes.name: Introduce the Green's function and corrector of $\Om$
nodes.statement: Let $G(\x,\y)$ denote the Green's function in $\Om$: \begin{align*} G(\x,\y)=\Phi(\y-\x)-H(\x,\y) \end{align*} where for each $\x\in\Om$, the corrector function $H(\x,\y)$ satisfies \begin{align*} \left\{\begin{array}{rclll} -\Delta_{\y} H(\x,\y)\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&0&\text{if}&\y\in\Om \vspace{0.125em}\\ H(\x,\y)\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&\Phi(\y-\x)&\text{if}&\y\in\p\Om. \end{array}\right. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Define $G=\Phi-H$ with the harmonic corrector $H$ matching $\Phi$ on the boundary.

nodes.name: Symmetry of the corrector function
nodes.statement: Note that since $G(\x,\y)=G(\y,\x)$ for $\x,\y\in\Om$ and $\Phi(\y-\x)=\Phi(\x-\y)$, we have $H(\x,\y)=H(\y,\x)$ for $\x,\y\in\Om$. Consequently, we have \begin{align} -\Delta_{\x}H(\x,\y)=-\Delta_{\x}H(\y,\x)=0~~~~~\x\in\Om. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Symmetry of $G$ and $\Phi$ makes $H$ symmetric, hence harmonic in its first argument.

nodes.name: Green's representation of the measured local field
nodes.statement: Then the solution to \cref{LBV} is represented as \begin{align*} b_l(\x)=\int_{\Om}G(\x,\y)P(D_{\y})\chi(\y)\rd\y=\int_{\Om}\Phi(\x-\y)P(D_{\y})\chi(\y)\rd\y+\mH(\x) \end{align*} where we used the fact that $\Phi(\y-\x)=\Phi(\x-\y)$, and $\mH(\x)$ is defined as \begin{align*} \mH(\x)=-\int_{\Om}H(\x,\y)P(D_{\y})\chi(\y)\rd\y \end{align*} for $\x\in\Om$. Then we can see that $\mH(\x)$ satisfies \begin{align} \left\{\begin{array}{rcll} -\Delta\mH\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&0&\text{in}~\Om \vspace{0.125em}\\ \mH\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&-\wt{b}_l&\text{on}~\p\Om \end{array}\right. \end{align} where the first equation of \cref{H_HarmonicEq} comes from \cref{CorrectorHarmonicSym}. Here, $\wt{b}_l$ is induced by the information of $\chi$ only in $\Om$: \begin{align} \wt{b}_l(\x)=\int_{\Om}\Phi(\x-\y)P(D_{\y})\chi(\y)\rd\y=\int_{\R^3}\Phi(\x-\y)1_{\Om}(\y)P(D_{\y})\chi(\y)\rd\y \end{align} with $1_{\Om}$ being the characteristic function of $\Om$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $b_l$ as the Newtonian potential over $\Om$ plus a harmonic term $\mH$ with boundary data $-\wt{b}_l$.

nodes.name: Define the incompatibility $v$ inside and outside $\Om$
nodes.statement: Based on the fact that $b_l(\x)=0$ for $\x\in\R^3\setminus\overline{\Om}$, we define \begin{align*} v(\x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cccll} v_{\mathrm i}(\x)\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&\mH(\x)&\text{if}&\x\in\Om \vspace{0.125em}\\ v_{\mathrm e}(\x)\hspace{-0.65em}&=\hspace{-0.65em}&-\wt{b}_l(\x)&\text{if}&\x\notin\Om. \end{array}\right. \end{align*} Hence, we obtain \cref{NewModeling}, and we can further see that $v_{\mathrm i}$ and $v_{\mathrm e}$ satisfy \begin{align} -\Delta v_{\mathrm i}&=0~~~~~~\text{in } \Om \\ -\Delta v_{\mathrm e}&=0~~~~~~\text{in } \R^3\setminus\overline{\Om} \\ v_{\mathrm i}=v_{\mathrm e}&=-\wt{b}_l~~~\text{on } \p\Om, \end{align} respectively, where \cref{v_eharmonic} comes from \cref{TrueLocalField}; $-\Delta\wt{b}_l=1_{\Om}P(D)\chi$, i.e. $-\Delta\wt{b}_l=P(D)\chi$ in $\Om$, and $-\Delta\wt{b}_l=0$ in $\R^3\setminus\overline{\Om}$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $v=\mH$ inside and $v=-\wt{b}_l$ outside, and record that both pieces are harmonic and agree on $\p\Om$.

nodes.name: Green's identity gives the distributional Laplacian of $v$
nodes.statement: To prove \cref{DistLapIncompatibility}, let $\varphi\in C_0^{\infty}(\R^3)$, and we consider \begin{align*} \int_{\R^3}v(\x)\left(-\Delta\varphi\right)(\x)\rd\x&=\int_{\Om}v_{\mathrm i}(\x)\left(-\Delta\varphi\right)(\x)\rd\x+\int_{\R^3\setminus\overline{\Om}}v_{\mathrm e}(\x)\left(-\Delta\varphi\right)(\x)\rd\x\\ &=I_1+I_2 \end{align*} Using \cref{v_iharmonic,vboundaryconti} and the Green's identity (e.g. \cite{Evans2010}), we have \begin{align*} I_1&=\int_{\Om}\left[\varphi(\x)\left(\Delta v_{\mathrm i}\right)(\x)-v_{\mathrm i}(\x)\left(\Delta\varphi\right)(\x)\right]\rd\x\\ &=\int_{\p\Om}\left[\varphi(\x)\f{\p v_{\mathrm i}}{\p\bn}(\x)-v_{\mathrm i}(\x)\f{\p\varphi}{\p\bn}(\x)\right]\rd\ssi(\x)=\int_{\p\Om}\left[\varphi(\x)\f{\p v_{\mathrm i}}{\p\bn}(\x)+\wt{b}_l(\x)\f{\p\varphi}{\p\bn}(\x)\right]\rd\ssi(\x). \end{align*} Similarly using \cref{v_eharmonic,vboundaryconti}, we also have \begin{align*} I_2&=\int_{\R^3\setminus\overline{\Om}}\left[\varphi(\x)\left(\Delta v_{\mathrm e}\right)(\x)-v_{\mathrm e}(\x)\left(\Delta\varphi\right)(\x)\right]\rd\x\\ &=\int_{\p\Om}\left[-\varphi(\x)\f{\p v_{\mathrm e}}{\p\bn}(\x)+v_{\mathrm e}(\x)\f{\p\varphi}{\p\bn}(\x)\right]\rd\ssi(\x)=-\int_{\p\Om}\left[\varphi(\x)\f{\p v_{\mathrm e}}{\p\bn}(\x)+\wt{b}_l(\x)\f{\p\varphi}{\p\bn}(\x)\right]\rd\ssi(\x) \end{align*} where the second equality comes from the fact that we need to compute the inward normal derivatives on $\p\Om$. Hence, combining these two equalities, we obtain \cref{DistLapIncompatibility}.
nodes.statement_short: Split the pairing into interior and exterior integrals and apply Green's identity to each.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data

nodes.name: Nonvanishing of the jump by contradiction and analyticity
nodes.statement: To prove 2, we assume on the contrary that there exists $\x\in\p\Om$ such that \begin{align*} \f{\p v_{\mathrm i}}{\p\bn}=\f{\p v_{\mathrm e}}{\p\bn} \end{align*} for some open and connected set $U\subseteq\p\Om$ such that $\x\in U$ and $\ssi(U)>0$. Choose $r>0$ such that $B(\x,r)\cap\p\Om$ is contained in $U$, where $B(\x,r)$ denotes an open ball centered at $\x$ with radius $r$. Then since $-\Delta v=0$ in $B(\x,r)$ and $v=v_{\mathrm e}=-\wt{b}_l$ in $B(\x,r)\cap\left(\R^3\setminus\overline{\Om}\right)$, it follows that $v=-\wt{b}_l$ in $B(\x,r)$ by the analyticity of $v$ in $B(\x,r)$. Since this means that $v=v_{\mathrm i}=-\wt{b}_l$ in $B(\x,r)\cap\Om$, together with the fact that $v_{\mathrm i}$ is harmonic in $\Om$, we have $v_{\mathrm i}=-\wt{b}_l$ in $\Om$ by the analyticity of $v_{\mathrm i}$ in $\Om$. Since $v=-\wt{b}_l$ on $\p\Om$, we have $v=-\wt{b}_l$ in $\R^3$. Hence, $-\Delta\wt{b}_l=0$ in $\R^3$, and thus, $P(D)\chi=0$ in $\Om$, which is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: If the normal derivatives agreed on a positive-measure patch, analyticity would force $P(D)\chi=0$ in $\Om$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data

nodes.name: True local field $\wt{b}_l$
nodes.statement: Here, $\wt{b}_l$ is induced by the information of $\chi$ only in $\Om$: \begin{align} \wt{b}_l(\x)=\int_{\Om}\Phi(\x-\y)P(D_{\y})\chi(\y)\rd\y=\int_{\R^3}\Phi(\x-\y)1_{\Om}(\y)P(D_{\y})\chi(\y)\rd\y \end{align} with $1_{\Om}$ being the characteristic function of $\Om$.
nodes.statement_short: The field induced by the susceptibility restricted to the ROI only.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data

nodes.name: Origin of the incompatibility in the boundary condition
nodes.statement: From the proof of \cref{Th1}, the incompatibility $v$ in \cref{NewModeling} is from the boundary condition of \cref{LBV} which is not related to the regularity of $\chi$. More precisely, $v_{\mathrm i}$ inside $\Om$ is generated by the information of the unknown true local field $\wt{b}_l$ on $\p\Om$ so that the boundary condition of \cref{LBV} is matched. In addition, it is obvious that $v_{\mathrm e}$ outside $\Om$ is due to the information loss outside $\Om$.
nodes.statement_short: The interior part of $v$ comes from matching the zero boundary condition; the exterior part from information loss outside $\Om$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data

nodes.name: $-\Delta v$ is a nonvanishing surface measure in QSM
nodes.statement: Notice that $P(D)$ is a ``wave type'' differential operator (by considering $x_3$ as the time variable). Indeed, the proof of \cref{NonVanishingSurfMeas} tells us that if $P(D)\chi=0$ in $\Om$, such $\chi$ has a wave type structure in $\Om$ regardless of its regularity, whereas the susceptibility of human brain does not have such a wave type structure \cite{J.K.Choi2014}. Hence in QSM, it follows that $-\Delta v$ defined as \cref{DistLapIncompatibility} is a nonvanishing surface measure on $\p\Om$, i.e. $-\Delta v=0$ in $\R^3\setminus\p\Om$, but $-\Delta v\neq0$ on $\p\Om$.
nodes.statement_short: Human-brain susceptibility has no wave-type structure, so the jump term never vanishes in practice.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data

nodes.name: Efficient solver of the Poisson equation for anisotropic resolution
nodes.statement: Since the real spatial resolution of phase data is not necessarily isotropic, an efficient and effective numerical solver of \cref{LBV} need to be investigated in the future, which is beyond the scope of this paper at this point.
nodes.statement_short: Designing a numerical solver of the background-removal Poisson problem that handles anisotropic voxels is left open.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data

nodes.name: Discrete image domain $\OO$, ROI $\Om$ and image space $\mI_3$
nodes.statement: We begin with introducing some notation. Let $\OO=\left\{0,\cdots,N_1-1\right\}\times\left\{0,\cdots,N_2-1\right\}\times\left\{0,\cdots,N_3-1\right\}$ denote the set of indices of $N_1\times N_2\times N_3$ grids, and let $\Om\subseteq\OO$ denote the set of indices corresponding to the ROI. Denote $\p\Om$ to be the indices of the boundary of ROI $\Om$. Finally, the space of real valued functions defined on $\OO$ is denoted as $\mI_3\simeq\R^{N_1\times N_2\times N_3}$.

nodes.name: Discrete forward model $b_l=A\chi+v+\eta$
nodes.statement: From the viewpoint of \cref{Th1}, we can model it as \begin{align*} b_l=A\chi+v+\eta \end{align*} where $A=\msF^{-1}\mD\msF$ denotes the discretization of the forward operator in \cref{NewModeling}. Here, $\chi\in\mI_3$ is the unknown true susceptibility image supported in $\Om$, $v\in\mI_3$ is the incompatibility arising from solving \cref{LBV}, and $\eta$ is the additive noise.
nodes.statement_short: Measured local field = discretized dipole operator applied to $\chi$, plus incompatibility, plus noise.

nodes.name: Discrete harmonic incompatibility condition
nodes.statement: We observe that in the discrete setting, \cref{DistLapIncompatibility} in \cref{Th1} can be understood as \begin{align} \msL v=0\quad\text{in}\quad\OO\setminus\p\Om\quad\text{ and }\quad \msL v\neq0\quad\text{on}\quad\p\Om \end{align} with the discrete Laplacian $\msL$, as $\msL v$ is supported on $\p\Om$.
nodes.statement_short: Discretely, $\msL v$ vanishes off the boundary and is nonzero on it, hence sparse.

nodes.name: Harmonic incompatibility removal (HIRE) model
nodes.statement: we assume the sparse approximation of $\chi$ under a given wavelet transformation $W$, and propose our HIRE model as follows: \begin{align} \min_{\chi,v\in\mI_3}~\f{1}{2}\left\|A\chi+v-b_l\right\|_{\Sigma}^2+\lambda\left\|\msL v\right\|_1+\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2} \end{align} where $\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\Sigma}^2=\left\la\Sigma\cdot,\cdot\right\ra$ with the SNR weight $\Sigma$ which is estimated from the MRI \cite{T.Liu2011a,C.Milovic2018}.
nodes.statement_short: Jointly recover $\chi$ and $v$ by minimizing a SNR-weighted fidelity plus $\ell_1$ penalties on $\msL v$ and on the frame coefficients of $\chi$.

nodes.name: Isotropic $\ell_1$ norm of wavelet frame coefficients
nodes.statement: Here, $\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2}$ is the isotropic $\ell_1$ norm of the wavelet frame coefficients \cite{J.F.Cai2012} defined as \begin{align} \left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2}:=\sum_{\bk\in\OO}\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\gamma_l[\bk]\left(\sum_{\aal\in\BB}\left|\left(W_{l,\aal}\chi\right)[\bk]\right|^2\right)^{1/2}. \end{align}
nodes.origin_citation: J. F. Cai, Dong, Osher & Shen 2012
nodes.definiendum: the isotropic $\ell_1$ norm of the wavelet frame coefficients

nodes.name: HIRE reduces to the integral and differential approaches
nodes.statement: For better understanding of our HIRE model, we temporarily assume that $\Sigma=I$ and consider \begin{align*} \min_{\chi,v\in\mI_3}~\f{1}{2}\left\|A\chi+v-b_l\right\|_2^2+\lambda\left\|\msL v\right\|_1+\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2}. \end{align*} If $v\equiv0$, our model reduces to the integral approach model: \begin{align*} \min_{\chi\in\mI_3}~\f{1}{2}\left\|A\chi-b_l\right\|_2^2+\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2}. \end{align*} In addition, if we fix $v=b_l-A\chi$, our model reduces to the $\ell_1$ fidelity version of the following differential approach model: \begin{align*} \min_{\chi\in\mI_3}~\f{1}{2}\left\|\msL b_l-\msL A\chi\right\|_2^2+\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2} \end{align*} as $\msL A\chi=\msL b_l$ discretizes the PDE \cref{QSM_PDE2} in the sense of \cite[Proposition A.1.]{J.K.Choi2014}.
nodes.statement_short: Setting $v\equiv0$ recovers the integral approach; fixing $v=b_l-A\chi$ recovers an $\ell_1$ differential approach.

nodes.name: Rank deficiency of the $\chi$ subproblem under variational regularization
nodes.statement: However, since $\mD(\0)=0$, the $\chi$ subproblem is a rank deficient system matrix, when using the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) methods \cite{J.Eckstein1992} to solve the regularization model. As a consequence, we may need additional prior information such as the zero susceptibility value in the cerebrospinal fluid region \cite{Z.Liu2017} for the stable reconstruction. In contrast, by using the tight frame regularization, the system matrix of $\chi$ subproblem has a full column rank, which can lead to the computational efficiency over the existing variational methods.
nodes.statement_short: Because $\mD(\0)=0$, TV/TGV models give a rank-deficient $\chi$ subproblem, while the tight frame gives full column rank.
conclusions: the $\chi$ subproblem is a rank deficient system matrix, when using the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) methods \cite{J.Eckstein1992} to solve the regularization model
by using the tight frame regularization, the system matrix of $\chi$ subproblem has a full column rank, which can lead to the computational efficiency over the existing variational methods

nodes.name: Nonlinear fidelity variants of the HIRE model
nodes.statement: We would like to mention that the formulation of HIRE model is not limited to \cref{WaveletFrameHIRE}. In fact, we can use the nonlinear fidelity term $F(b_l|\chi,v)=\f{1}{2}\left\|e^{i(A\chi+v)\om_0B_0TE}-e^{ib_l\om_0B_0TE}\right\|_{\Sigma}^2$ to further compensate the errors in phase unwrapping, which will be more coincident with the GRE signal model \cite{Y.Kee2017,T.Liu2013}. However, we will not discuss the details on such nonlinear variants as this is beyond the scope of this paper. We will focus on \cref{WaveletFrameHIRE} throughout this paper.
nodes.statement_short: A nonlinear phase-consistent fidelity is possible but is left outside the paper's scope.

nodes.name: Constrained reformulation of the HIRE model for split Bregman
nodes.statement: More precisely, let $d=W\chi$, $e=\msL v$, $f=A\chi$, and $g=v$. Then \cref{WaveletFrameHIRE} is reformulated as follows: \begin{align*} &\min_{\chi,v,d,e,f,g}~\f{1}{2}\left\|f+g-b_l\right\|_{\Sigma}^2+\lambda\left\|e\right\|_1+\left\|\gamma\cdot d\right\|_{1,2}\\ &\text{subject to}~d=W\chi,~e=\msL v,~f=A\chi,~\text{and}~g=v. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce splitting variables $d,e,f,g$ to turn the HIRE model into a linearly constrained problem.

nodes.name: Split Bregman Algorithm for the HIRE model
nodes.statement: \STATE{\textbf{Initialization:} $\chi^0$, $v^0$, $d^0$, $e^0$, $f^0$, $g^0$, $p^0$, $q^0$, $r^0$, $s^0$} \FOR{$k=0$, $1$, $2$, $\cdots$} \STATE{Update $\chi$ and $v$: \begin{align} \chi^{k+1}&=\argmin_{\chi}~\f{\beta}{2}\|A\chi-f^k+r^k\|_2^2+\f{\beta}{2}\|W\chi-d^k+p^k\|_2^2 \\ v^{k+1}&=\argmin_{v}~\f{\beta}{2}\|v-g^k+s^k\|_2^2+\f{\beta}{2}\|\msL v-e^k+q^k\|_2^2 \end{align} Update $d$, $e$, $f$, and $g$: \begin{align} d^{k+1}&=\argmin_d~\left\|\gamma\cdot d\right\|_{1,2}+\f{\beta}{2}\|d-W\chi^{k+1}-p^k\|_2^2 \\ e^{k+1}&=\argmin_e~\lambda\left\|e\right\|_1+\f{\beta}{2}\|e-\msL v^{k+1}-q^k\|_2^2 \\ f^{k+1}&=\argmin_f~\f{1}{2}\|f+g^k-b_l\|_{\Sigma}^2+\f{\beta}{2}\|f-A\chi^{k+1}-r^k\|_2^2 \\ g^{k+1}&=\argmin_g~\f{1}{2}\|g+f^{k+1}-b_l\|_{\Sigma}^2+\f{\beta}{2}\|g-v^{k+1}-s^k\|_2^2 \end{align} Update $p$, $q$, $r$, and $s$: \begin{align} p^{k+1}&=p^k+W\chi^{k+1}-d^{k+1} \\ q^{k+1}&=q^k+\msL v^{k+1}-e^{k+1} \\ r^{k+1}&=r^k+A\chi^{k+1}-f^{k+1} \\ s^{k+1}&=s^k+v^{k+1}-g^{k+1} \end{align}} \ENDFOR
nodes.statement_short: ADMM/split Bregman iteration alternating closed-form $\chi,v$ solves, soft thresholdings for $d,e$, diagonal solves for $f,g$, and Bregman multiplier updates.
input: $b_l\in\mI_3$ be the (noisy) measured local field data obtained from \cref{LBV}

nodes.name: Initialization of all primal and Bregman variables
nodes.statement_short: Initialize the susceptibility, incompatibility, splitting and multiplier variables.

nodes.name: Outer iteration loop
nodes.statement_short: Iterate over $k$.

nodes.name: Update $\chi$ and $v$
nodes.statement: \STATE{Update $\chi$ and $v$: \begin{align} \chi^{k+1}&=\argmin_{\chi}~\f{\beta}{2}\|A\chi-f^k+r^k\|_2^2+\f{\beta}{2}\|W\chi-d^k+p^k\|_2^2 \\ v^{k+1}&=\argmin_{v}~\f{\beta}{2}\|v-g^k+s^k\|_2^2+\f{\beta}{2}\|\msL v-e^k+q^k\|_2^2 \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Solve the two quadratic subproblems for the susceptibility and the incompatibility.

nodes.name: Update $d$, $e$, $f$, and $g$
nodes.statement: Update $d$, $e$, $f$, and $g$: \begin{align} d^{k+1}&=\argmin_d~\left\|\gamma\cdot d\right\|_{1,2}+\f{\beta}{2}\|d-W\chi^{k+1}-p^k\|_2^2 \\ e^{k+1}&=\argmin_e~\lambda\left\|e\right\|_1+\f{\beta}{2}\|e-\msL v^{k+1}-q^k\|_2^2 \\ f^{k+1}&=\argmin_f~\f{1}{2}\|f+g^k-b_l\|_{\Sigma}^2+\f{\beta}{2}\|f-A\chi^{k+1}-r^k\|_2^2 \\ g^{k+1}&=\argmin_g~\f{1}{2}\|g+f^{k+1}-b_l\|_{\Sigma}^2+\f{\beta}{2}\|g-v^{k+1}-s^k\|_2^2 \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Soft-threshold the frame and Laplacian variables and solve the two fidelity subproblems.

nodes.name: Update the Bregman multipliers $p$, $q$, $r$, and $s$
nodes.statement: Update $p$, $q$, $r$, and $s$: \begin{align} p^{k+1}&=p^k+W\chi^{k+1}-d^{k+1} \\ q^{k+1}&=q^k+\msL v^{k+1}-e^{k+1} \\ r^{k+1}&=r^k+A\chi^{k+1}-f^{k+1} \\ s^{k+1}&=s^k+v^{k+1}-g^{k+1} \end{align}}
nodes.statement_short: Add the current constraint residuals to the four Bregman multipliers.

nodes.name: Closed form solutions of the $\chi$ and $v$ subproblems
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that each subproblem has a closed form solution. The solutions to \cref{chisubproblem,vsubproblem} can be written as \begin{align} \chi^{k+1}&=\big(A^TA+I\big)^{-1}\big[A^T(f^k-r^k)+W^T(d^k-p^k)\big] \\ v^{k+1}&=\big(I+\msL^T\msL\big)^{-1}\big[g^k-s^k+\msL^T(e^k-q^k)\big]. \end{align} Since we use the periodic boundary conditions, both \cref{chisubexplicit,vsubexplicit} can be easily solved by using the fast Fourier transform.
nodes.statement_short: Both subproblems reduce to inverting $A^TA+I$ and $I+\msL^T\msL$, diagonal under periodic boundary conditions, so FFT solves them.
assumptions: Since we use the periodic boundary conditions
conclusions: each subproblem has a closed form solution
both \cref{chisubexplicit,vsubexplicit} can be easily solved by using the fast Fourier transform

nodes.name: Isotropic soft thresholding $\mT_{\gamma}$
nodes.statement: Here, $\mT_{\gamma}$ is the isotropic soft thresholding in \cite{J.F.Cai2012}: given $d$ defined as \begin{align*} d=\left\{d_{l,\aal}:(l,\aal)\in\left(\left\{0,\cdots,L-1\right\}\times\BB\right)\cup\left\{(L-1,\0)\right\}\right\} \end{align*} and $\gamma=\left\{\gamma_l:l=0,1,\cdots,L-1\right\}$ with $\gamma_l\geq0$, $\mT_{\gamma}\left(d\right)$ is defined as \begin{align*} \left(\mT_{\gamma}\left(d\right)\right)_{l,\aal}[\bk]=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} d_{l,\aal}[\bk],&(l,\aal)=(L-1,\0)\vspace{0.125em}\\ \displaystyle{\max\left(R_l[\bk]-\gamma_l[\bk],0\right)\f{d_{l,\aal}[\bk]}{R_l[\bk]}},&(l,\aal)\in\left\{0,\cdots,L-1\right\}\times\BB \end{array}\right. \end{align*} where $R_l[\bk]=\left(\sum_{\aal\in\BB}\left|d_{l,\aal}[\bk]\right|^2\right)^{1/2}$ for $\bk\in\OO$.
nodes.statement_short: Groupwise shrinkage of framelet coefficients by band magnitude, leaving the lowpass band untouched.
nodes.origin_citation: J. F. Cai, Dong, Osher & Shen 2012

nodes.name: Soft thresholding solutions of the $d$ and $e$ subproblems
nodes.statement: In addition, the solutions to \cref{dsubproblem,esubproblem} are expressed in terms of the soft thresholding: \begin{align} d^{k+1}&=\mT_{\gamma/\beta}\big(W\chi^{k+1}+p^k\big) \\ e^{k+1}&=\max\big(|\msL v^{k+1}+q^k|-\lambda/\beta,0\big)\sign\big(\msL v^{k+1}+q^k\big). \end{align}

nodes.name: Closed form solutions of the $f$ and $g$ subproblems
nodes.statement: Finally, the solutions to \cref{fsubproblem,gsubproblem} are expressed as \begin{align} f^{k+1}&=\big(\Sigma+\beta I\big)^{-1}\big[\Sigma(b_l-g^k)+\beta(A\chi^{k+1}+r^k)\big] \\ g^{k+1}&=\big(\Sigma+\beta I\big)^{-1}\big[\Sigma(b_l-f^{k+1})+\beta(v^{k+1}+s^k)\big] \end{align} where $\Sigma+\beta I$ is simply a diagonal matrix and thus, no matrix inversion is needed.
nodes.statement_short: Both are diagonal solves because $\Sigma+\beta I$ is diagonal.

nodes.name: Convergence of the split Bregman algorithm for the HIRE model
nodes.statement: Note that, since our model \cref{WaveletFrameHIRE} is convex, it can be verified that \cref{Algorithm1} converges to the minimizer of \cref{WaveletFrameHIRE} by following the framework of \cite[Theorem 3.2.]{J.F.Cai2009/10}, whenever it has the unique global minimizer.
nodes.statement_short: Convexity plus the framework of Cai, Osher & Shen yields convergence to the minimizer.
assumptions: whenever it has the unique global minimizer

nodes.name: Wavelet frame integral approach (Frame-Int)
nodes.statement: the wavelet frame integral approach (Frame-Int) \begin{align} \min_{\chi\in\mI_3}~\f{1}{2}\left\|A\chi-b_l\right\|_{\Sigma}^2+\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Integral-approach baseline: SNR-weighted dipole fidelity plus isotropic framelet $\ell_1$ penalty.

nodes.name: Wavelet frame differential approach (Frame-Diff)
nodes.statement: and the wavelet frame differential approach (Frame-Diff) \begin{align} \min_{\chi\in\mI_3}~\f{1}{2}\left\|\msL A\chi-\msL b_l\right\|_{\Sigma}^2+\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2} \end{align} where the SNR weight for \cref{WaveletFrameDifferential} is estimated by the method described in \cite{Y.Kee2017}.
nodes.statement_short: Differential-approach baseline: Laplacian-preconditioned fidelity plus isotropic framelet $\ell_1$ penalty.

nodes.statement:
we also test the models by replacing $\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chiight\|_{1,2}$ in \cref{WaveletFrameHIRE,WaveletFrameIntegral,WaveletFrameDifferential} into the following TGV term:  egin{align} \mathrm{TGV}_{\alpha_1,\alpha_0}^2(\chi)=\alpha_1\left\|
a\chi-pight\|_1+\alpha_0\left\|\mE pight\|_1,~~~	ext{where}~~\mE= {1}{2}\left(
a+
a^Tight), \end{align} which will be denoted as TGV-HIRE, TGV-Int and TGV-Diff respectively.

nodes.name: Stopping criterion of the split Bregman iterations
nodes.statement: The stopping criterion for \cref{Algorithm1} is \begin{align*} \f{\|\chi^{k+1}-\chi^k\|_2}{\|\chi^{k+1}\|_2}\leq5\times10^{-3}, \end{align*}

nodes.name: Frame-HIRE and TGV-HIRE outperform direct, integral and differential approaches
nodes.statement: We can see that both the Frame-HIRE and the TGV-HIRE consistently outperform the existing direct approaches, the integral approaches, and the differential approaches in both cases. At first glance, this verifies the convention that the regularization based models in general performs better in solving the ill-posed inverse problem of QSM than the direct methods \cite{Y.Kee2017,S.Wang2013}. Most importantly, this result demonstrates that the measured local field data obtained from the phase of a complex GRE MR signal contains the harmonic incompatibility other than the noise, which agrees with our theoretical discovery, and the performance gain mainly comes from taking both the noise in the measured data and the harmonic incompatibility (the incompatibility other than the noise) at the same time.
nodes.statement_short: On the brain phantom the HIRE models beat all baselines, supporting the claim that the measured local field carries a harmonic incompatibility.
assumptions: \cref{ComparisonTableFra} summarizes the relative error and the SSIM of the direct approaches (\cref{TKD,Tikhonov}) and the wavelet frame regularization approaches
conclusions: both the Frame-HIRE and the TGV-HIRE consistently outperform the existing direct approaches, the integral approaches, and the differential approaches in both cases
the measured local field data obtained from the phase of a complex GRE MR signal contains the harmonic incompatibility other than the noise

nodes.name: Frame-HIRE is computationally preferable to TGV-HIRE
nodes.statement: In addition, since $\mD(\0)=0$, the $\chi$ subproblem of the TGV-HIRE has a rank deficient system matrix due to the constant offset, unlike the Frame-HIRE whose system matrix has a full column rank due to $W^TW=I$. As a consequence, the CPU time of the TGV-HIRE becomes approximately $3$ times longer than approximately $11.5\mathrm{min}$ of the Frame-HIRE as shown in \cref{ComparisonTimePhantom}, which shows that the TGV regularization approach may not be suitable for the real clinical applications. Therefore, even though it is approximately $1.9$ times slower than the Frame-Int, we can nevertheless conclude that compared to the TGV-HIRE, the Frame-HIRE is able to achieve the efficiency of its split Bregman algorithm as well as the shadow and streaking artifact removal.
nodes.statement_short: TGV-HIRE is roughly three times slower and oversmoothed, so the framelet version is preferable in practice.
assumptions: since $\mD(\0)=0$, the $\chi$ subproblem of the TGV-HIRE has a rank deficient system matrix due to the constant offset
conclusions: the CPU time of the TGV-HIRE becomes approximately $3$ times longer than approximately $11.5\mathrm{min}$ of the Frame-HIRE
the Frame-HIRE is able to achieve the efficiency of its split Bregman algorithm as well as the shadow and streaking artifact removal

nodes.name: HIRE suppresses streaking artifacts propagating from $\p\Om$
nodes.statement: It is also worth noting that the HIRE models can reduce the streaking artifacts which propagate from $\p\Om$ into $\Om$ as well as the shadow artifacts. As pointed out in \cite{Y.Wang2015}, the in vivo local field data is prone to the outliers near $\p\Om$ because the GRE signal lacks information outside $\Om$. Hence, we can see that most streaking artifacts propagate from these outliers near $\p\Om$ into the ROI. However, thanks to the sparsity promoting property of $\ell_1$ norm, the term $\lambda\left\|\msL v\right\|_1$ in the HIRE approaches can somehow capture and remove them, leading to the suppression of artifacts propagating from $\p\Om$ into $\Om$ as well as the shadow and streaking artifact removal.
nodes.statement_short: The $\ell_1$ penalty on $\msL v$ captures boundary outliers, removing artifacts that propagate inward from $\p\Om$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Experiments on In Vivo MR Data
assumptions: the in vivo local field data is prone to the outliers near $\p\Om$ because the GRE signal lacks information outside $\Om$
conclusions: the HIRE models can reduce the streaking artifacts which propagate from $\p\Om$ into $\Om$ as well as the shadow artifacts

nodes.name: Quasi-affine system $\msX(\Ps)$
nodes.statement: For a given $\Ps=\left\{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_r\right\}\subseteq L_2(\R^d)$ with $d\in\N$, a quasi-affine system $\msX(\Ps)$ generated by $\Ps$ is the collection of the dilations and the shifts of the elements in $\Ps$: \begin{align} \msX(\Ps)=\left\{\psi_{\alpha,n,\bk}:1\leq\alpha\leq r,~n\in\Z,~\bk\in\Z^d\right\}, \end{align} where $\psi_{\alpha,n,\bk}$ is defined as \begin{align} \psi_{\alpha,n,\bk}=\left\{\begin{array}{cl} 2^{\f{nd}{2}}\psi_{\alpha}(2^n\cdot-\bk)~~&~~n\geq 0;\vspace{0.125em}\\ 2^{nd}\psi_{\alpha}(2^n\cdot-2^{n}\bk)~~&~~n<0. \end{array}\right. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: All dyadic dilations and shifts of a generator set, undecimated below scale zero.
nodes.genus: the collection of the dilations and the shifts of the elements in $\Ps$

nodes.name: Tight wavelet frame
nodes.statement: We say that $\msX(\Ps)$ is a tight wavelet frame on $L_2(\R^d)$ if we have \begin{align} \left\|f\right\|_{L_2(\R^d)}^2=\sum_{\alpha=1}^r\sum_{n\in\Z}\sum_{\bk\in\Z^d}\left|\left\la f,\psi_{\alpha,n,\bk}\right\ra\right|^2 \end{align} for every $f\in L_2(\R^d)$. In this case, each $\psi_{\alpha}$ is called a (tight) framelet, and $\left\la f,\psi_{\alpha,n,\bk}\right\ra$ is called the canonical coefficient of $f$.

nodes.name: MRA based construction: refinement mask and wavelet frame masks
nodes.statement: The constructions of (anti-)symmetric and compactly supported framelets $\Ps$ are usually based on a multiresolution analysis (MRA); we first find some compactly supported refinable function $\phi$ with a refinement mask $q_0$ such that \begin{align} \phi=2^d\sum_{\bk\in\Z^d}q_0[\bk]\phi(2\cdot-\bk). \end{align} Then the MRA based construction of $\Ps=\left\{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_r\right\}\subseteq L_2(\R^d)$ is to find finitely supported masks $q_{\alpha}$ such that \begin{align} \psi_{\alpha}=2^d\sum_{\bk\in\Z^d}q_{\alpha}[\bk]\phi(2\cdot-\bk),~~~~~\alpha=1,\cdots,r. \end{align} The sequences $q_1,\cdots,q_r$ are called wavelet frame mask or the high pass filters of the system, and the refinement mask $q_0$ is also called the low pass filter.
nodes.statement_short: Framelets are built from a refinable function and finitely supported high pass masks $q_1,\dots,q_r$.
nodes.origin_citation: A. Ron & Z. Shen 1997; B. Dong & Shen 2013

nodes.name: Unitary extension principle (UEP)
nodes.statement: The unitary extension principle (UEP) of \cite{A.Ron1997} provides a general theory of the construction of MRA based tight wavelet frames. Briefly speaking, as long as $\left\{q_0,q_1,\cdots,q_r\right\}$ are compactly supported and their Fourier series $\wh{q}_{\alpha}(\xxi)=\sum_{\bk\in\Z^d}q_{\alpha}[\bk]e^{-i\xxi\cdot\bk}$ satisfy \begin{align} \sum_{\alpha=0}^r\left|\wh{q}_{\alpha}(\xxi)\right|^2=1~~~~\text{and}~~~~\sum_{\alpha=0}^r\wh{q}_{\alpha}(\xxi)\overline{\wh{q}_{\alpha}(\xxi+\nnu)}=0 \end{align} for all $\nnu\in\left\{0,\pi\right\}^d\setminus\left\{\0\right\}$ and $\xxi\in[-\pi,\pi]^d$, the quasi-affine system $\msX(\Ps)$ with $\Ps=\left\{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_r\right\}$ defined by \cref{MRA-Fra} forms a tight frame of $L_2(\R^d)$, and the filters $\left\{q_0,q_1,\cdots,q_r\right\}$ form a discrete tight frame on $\ell_2(\Z^d)$ \cite{B.Dong2013}.
nodes.statement_short: If the masks are compactly supported and their Fourier series satisfy the UEP identities, the MRA system is a tight frame.
assumptions: as long as $\left\{q_0,q_1,\cdots,q_r\right\}$ are compactly supported and their Fourier series $\wh{q}_{\alpha}(\xxi)=\sum_{\bk\in\Z^d}q_{\alpha}[\bk]e^{-i\xxi\cdot\bk}$ satisfy
conclusions: the quasi-affine system $\msX(\Ps)$ with $\Ps=\left\{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_r\right\}$ defined by \cref{MRA-Fra} forms a tight frame of $L_2(\R^d)$
the filters $\left\{q_0,q_1,\cdots,q_r\right\}$ form a discrete tight frame on $\ell_2(\Z^d)$

nodes.name: Piecewise constant B-spline (Haar framelet)
nodes.statement: The piecewise constant B-spline (or the Haar framelet) \cite{I.Daubechies2003} for $L_2(\R)$ has one refinable function and one framelet \begin{align*} \phi(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ccl} 1&\text{if}&x\in[0,1)\vspace{0.125em}\\ 0&\text{if}&x\notin[0,1) \end{array}\right.~~~\text{and}~~~\psi_1(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ccl} 1&\text{if}&x\in[0,1/2)\vspace{0.125em}\\ -1&\text{if}&x\in[1/2,1)\vspace{0.125em}\\ 0&\text{if}&x\notin[0,1) \end{array}\right. \end{align*} as shown in \cref{IllustrateExA1}. Here, the associated filters are \begin{align*} q_0=\f{1}{2}\big[\begin{array}{cc} 1&1 \end{array}\big]~~~\text{and}~~~q_1=\f{1}{2}\big[\begin{array}{cc} 1&-1 \end{array}\big]. \end{align*} Since this $\left\{q_0,q_1\right\}$ satisfies \cref{UEP}, $\msX\left(\Ps\right)$ with $\Ps=\left\{\psi_1\right\}$ forms a tight frame on $L_2(\R)$.
nodes.statement_short: The Haar refinable function and framelet with filters $\tfrac12[1\ 1]$ and $\tfrac12[1\ -1]$ satisfy UEP.

nodes.name: Tensor product construction of multivariate tight framelets
nodes.statement: The tight frame on $L_2(\R^d)$ with $d\geq 2$ can be constructed by taking tensor products of univariate tight framelets \cite{J.F.Cai2012,J.F.Cai2016,Daubechies1992,B.Dong2013}. Given a set of univariate masks $\big\{q_0,q_1,\cdots,q_r\big\}$, we define multivariate masks $q_{\aal}[\bk]$ with $\aal=(\alpha_1,\cdots,\alpha_d)$ and $\bk=(k_1,\cdots,k_d)$ as \begin{align*} q_{\aal}[\bk]=q_{\alpha_1}[k_1]\cdots q_{\alpha_d}[k_d],~~~~~~0\leq\alpha_1,\cdots,\alpha_d\leq r,~~\bk=(k_1,\cdots,k_d)\in\Z^d. \end{align*} The corresponding multivariate refinable function and framelets are defined as \begin{align*} \psi_{\aal}(\x)=\psi_{\alpha_1}(x_1)\cdots\psi_{\alpha_d}(x_d),~~~~~0\leq\alpha_1,\cdots,\alpha_d\leq r,~~\x=(x_1,\cdots,x_d)\in\R^d \end{align*} with $\psi_0=\phi$ for convenience. If the univariate masks $\left\{q_{\alpha}\right\}$ are constructed from UEP, then we can verify that $\left\{q_{\aal}\right\}$ satisfies \cref{UEP} and thus $\msX(\Ps)$ with $\Ps=\left\{\psi_{\aal}:\aal\in\{0,\cdots,r\}^d\setminus\{\0\}\right\}$ forms a tight frame for $L_2(\R^d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Tensor products of UEP univariate masks again satisfy UEP, giving a tight frame in $d$ dimensions.
nodes.origin_citation: J. F. Cai et al. 2012; Daubechies 1992; B. Dong & Shen 2013
assumptions: If the univariate masks $\left\{q_{\alpha}\right\}$ are constructed from UEP
conclusions: $\msX(\Ps)$ with $\Ps=\left\{\psi_{\aal}:\aal\in\{0,\cdots,r\}^d\setminus\{\0\}\right\}$ forms a tight frame for $L_2(\R^d)$

nodes.name: Fast framelet decomposition (analysis operator $W$)
nodes.statement: In the discrete setting, let $\mI_d\simeq\R^{N_1\times\cdots\times N_d}$ be the space of real valued functions defined on a regular grid $\left\{0,1,\cdots,N_1-1\right\}\times\cdots\times\left\{0,1,\cdots,N_d-1\right\}$. The fast framelet decomposition, or the analysis operator with $L$ levels of decomposition is defined as \begin{align} Wu=\left\{W_{l,\aal}u:(l,\aal)\in\left(\left\{0,\cdots,L-1\right\}\times\BB\right)\cup\left\{(L-1,\0)\right\}\right\} \end{align} where $\BB=\left\{0,\cdots,r\right\}^d\setminus\left\{\0\right\}$ is the framelet band. Then the frame coefficients $W_{l,\aal}u\in\mI_d$ of $u\in\mI_d$ at level $l$ and band $\aal$ are defined as \begin{align*} W_{l,\aal}u=q_{l,\aal}[-\cdot]\circledast u. \end{align*} where $\circledast$ denotes the discrete convolution with a certain boundary condition (e.g. the periodic boundary condition), and $q_{l,\aal}$ is defined as \begin{align} q_{l,\aal}=\wt{q}_{l,\aal}\circledast\wt{q}_{l-1,\0}\circledast\cdots\circledast\wt{q}_{0,\0}~~\text{with}~~\wt{q}_{l,\aal}[\bk]=\left\{\begin{array}{cl} q_{\aal}[2^{-l}\bk],&\bk\in 2^l\Z^d\vspace{0.125em}\\ 0,&\bk\notin 2^l\Z^d. \end{array}\right. \end{align} We denote by $W^T$, the adjoint of $W$, the fast reconstruction (or the synthesis operator).
nodes.statement_short: Discrete framelet coefficients are convolutions with the level-$l$, band-$\aal$ masks; $W^T$ is the synthesis operator.
nodes.origin_citation: J. F. Cai et al. 2012; B. Dong & Shen 2013
nodes.definiendum: the analysis operator with $L$ levels of decomposition

nodes.name: Perfect reconstruction $W^TW=I$
nodes.statement: Then by UEP \cref{UEP}, we have $W^TW=I$.

nodes.name: Choice of the framelet system
nodes.statement: Finally, we mention that among many different choice of framelets, the ones constructed from the B-spline are the most popular in image processing. This is due to the multiscale structure of the wavelet frame systems, short supports of the (anti-)symmetric framelet functions with varied vanishing moments, and the presence of both low pass and high pass filters in the wavelet frame filter banks, which are desirable in sparsely approximating images \cite{B.Dong2017a}. A tight frame system constructed from the low order B-spline has fewer filters with shorter supports compared to the ones constructed from the high order B-splines. Hence, low order B-spline framelet systems are more computationally efficient while the high order ones are capable of capturing richer image singularities. Moreover, since high order B-spline framelets have larger supports, they may introduce more numerical viscosity, often leading to smoother reconstructions in image restoration tasks. Hence, the choice of framelet systems indeed depends on the the task and the computational cost we can afford \cite{H.Zhang2018}. In this paper, we fix $W$ to be the Haar framelet system for the wavelet frame regularization models as the susceptibility images can be well approximated by piecewise constant functions. Besides, we always fix $L=1$ to avoid the memory storage problem as we solve three dimensional inverse problem. We also note that the choices of $W$ will indeed affect the reconstruction results. For example, the use of data driven tight frames in \cite{J.F.Cai2014} will generate better reconstruction results due to its adaptivity, even though it requires further numerical studies. Nonetheless, we forgo more details on the choice of $W$ in order not to dilute the main focus of this paper.
nodes.statement_short: Low-order B-spline framelets are cheaper, high-order ones capture richer singularities; the paper fixes Haar with $L=1$.
